summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Department of Children & Families v. A.L.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed an abuse-or-neglect finding based on prenatal cocaine use, holding Title 9 requires competent proof of actual harm to the child or of imminent danger or substantial risk of harm.
key_cases.relevance: A.L. requires evidence of actual harm or imminent danger, the same showing that must underlie an emergency removal.
key_cases.quote: If an expectant mother's drug use causes actual harm to the physical, mental, or emotional condition of a newborn child, a finding of abuse or neglect is appropriate.

key_cases.holding: The Court upheld an order taking temporary custody of an infant and authorizing a blood transfusion over the parents' religious objection, finding no federal or state constitutional violation.
key_cases.relevance: Perricone shows the parens patriae basis on which the State may act immediately to protect a child's life.
key_cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that neither N. J. S. A. 9:2-9 nor the action of the trial court pursuant to the statute is violative of either the Federal or the State Constitution.

key_cases.case_name: L.A. v. New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court defined the standard governing a physician's statutory duty to report, holding 'reasonable cause to believe' exists when a probable inference from the available information is that the child's condition results from abuse.
key_cases.relevance: L.A. supplies the inference standard that separates actionable suspicion from speculation before the State intervenes.
key_cases.quote: The inference need not be the "most probable," but it must be more than speculation or suspicion.

key_cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's constitutional right to integrity because there were no objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Croft sets the evidentiary floor a caseworker must have before effecting an emergency separation.
key_cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit.

key_cases.case_name: Mammaro v. New Jersey Division of Child Protection & Permanency
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of qualified immunity to New Jersey caseworkers, holding no clearly established law made the temporary removal of a child on these allegations a substantive due process violation.
key_cases.relevance: Mammaro shows the narrow margin between a contestable removal decision and one that defeats immunity.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, no Supreme Court precedent clearly establishes that D.M.'s temporary removal from her mother's custody violated substantive due process.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the dependency adjudication, holding that an unwed father was entitled under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses to a hearing on his fitness before the State could take his children from him.
key_cases.relevance: Stanley requires an individualized determination of parental fitness rather than a presumption, and fixes the hearing the State owes when it takes custody.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately upon receipt of the report; investigation initiated within 24 hours
timeline_requirements.starts_from: The Division's receipt of a report of child abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.11; a delay in initiating the investigation is permitted only where the Division or other designated entity authorizes it at the request of a law enforcement official.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: State Central Registry assigns the CPS report to the local office for response
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Good cause must be established and an extension approved by the local office manager or designee before day 60 (CP&P-II-C-6-200).
